q: A 78-year-old man with a history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia presents with vesicular lesions involving several dermatomes over his trunk and back. He completed CLL treatment two years ago and remains in remission. His CD4+ count is 180 cells/μL. Which immune impairment is most relevant to susceptibility to herpes zoster in this presentation?
o: Impairment of humoral immunity and antibody production
Impairment of neutrophil function and directed chemotaxis
Impairment of VZV-specific T-cell-mediated immunity
Impairment of complement-system activation and function
explanation:
Control of latent varicella-zoster virus relies particularly on cellular immunity. Multidermatomal zoster and a low CD4 count point to **impaired VZV-specific T-cell-mediated immunity**.

**A. Humoral immunity.** Antibody deficiency can occur in CLL, but it is not the main mechanism controlling latent VZV.
**B. Neutrophil chemotaxis.** Neutrophils are important in other infections. A low CD4 count identifies a different immune compartment.
**C. VZV-specific T cells.** Weak cellular surveillance allows latent virus to reactivate and can accompany more extensive zoster.
**D. Complement activation.** Complement deficiency is not the characteristic immune defect in this presentation.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 60, 1724.
ref: Hazzard Ch 107 — OTHER VIRUSES: HUMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS INFECTION AND HERPES ZOSTER
chapterTitle: Other Viruses: Human Immunodeficiency Virus Infection and Herpes Zoster

. VZV-specific T cells.** Weak cellular surveillance allows latent virus to reactivate and can accompany more extensive zoster.

q: חולה נוטה למות אינה כשירה ואין הנחיות מקדימות זמינות. הרופא האחראי בודק את רצונה ביחס להחייאה בשלב זה. איזה מידע ניתן להביא בחשבון לפי חוק החולה הנוטה למות?
o: עמדת הבן הבכור לגבי הטיפול הרצוי לו
עמדת רוב בני המשפחה לפי הצבעה
הצהרה מפורשת של אדם קרוב על רצונה
בחירת המטפל העיקרי לפי העדפתו האישית
explanation:
אדם קרוב יכול להצהיר על רצונה של המטופלת. הרופא האחראי בוחן את התנאים החוקיים ואת המידע על רצונה. למזון, לנוזלים ולטיפול נלווה יש כללים נפרדים.

אסמכתא · Israeli Dying Patient Law §§5,16–17.

q: A patient on morphine becomes somnolent during acute kidney injury. Which mechanism increases the risk of delayed opioid toxicity?
o: Reduced renal clearance of active morphine metabolites
Increased sequestration of morphine in adipose tissue
Accelerated conversion of morphine to inactive products
Reduced enteric uptake of the next morphine dose
explanation:
**A.** Morphine glucuronides depend on renal elimination. Their accumulation during kidney injury can cause persistent sedation and respiratory depression even after dosing stops.
**B.** Adipose distribution does not account for the renal dependence of active morphine metabolites.
**C.** Inactivation alone would tend to reduce opioid effects rather than prolong them.
**D.** Less absorption does not explain toxicity during loss of kidney function.

q: A 79-year-old woman with mild cognitive impairment, anxiety, and insomnia is having cataract surgery with monitored anesthesia care. Her medications include escitalopram and zolpidem. Which proposed sedative is specifically marked in Hazzard’s anesthesia-drug table as one to avoid in older patients because it contributes to postoperative delirium?
o: Propofol
Dexmedetomidine
Midazolam
Remifentanil
explanation:
Pre-existing cognitive impairment increases vulnerability to postoperative delirium. **Midazolam**, a benzodiazepine, is the sedative specifically flagged for avoidance when possible.

**A. Propofol.** Propofol is a rapidly acting IV anesthetic with dose-related respiratory and cardiovascular effects.
**B. Dexmedetomidine.** Dexmedetomidine provides sedation through alpha-2 agonism and can cause bradycardia and hypotension.
**C. Midazolam.** Midazolam can worsen attention and memory and contribute to postoperative delirium.
**D. Remifentanil.** Remifentanil is a short-acting opioid with respiratory effects, a different drug class and concern.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 386, 387, 390.

. Dexmedetomidine.** Dexmedetomidine provides sedation through alpha-2 agonism and can cause bradycardia and hypotension.
. Midazolam.** Midazolam can worsen attention and memory and contribute to postoperative delirium.
. Remifentanil.** Remifentanil is a short-acting opioid with respiratory effects, a different drug class and concern.

explanationParts.text: Pre-existing cognitive impairment increases vulnerability to postoperative delirium. **Midazolam**, a benzodiazepine, is the sedative specifically flagged for avoidance when possible.

q: A 79-year-old man with diabetes and mild cognitive impairment has lost about 7 kg in four months. He takes small bites, chews extensively, reports food going 'the wrong way,' and has a wet, gurgly voice after meals. Medications are metformin 500 mg twice daily, glipizide 10 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg daily; creatinine clearance is 44 mL/min. Modified barium swallow shows vallecular residue and delayed swallow initiation. Which statement correctly characterizes rehabilitative swallowing therapy considered after this assessment?
o: Adjust mealtime lighting and cueing.
Change bolus volume or consistency.
Train swallowing muscles to improve physiologic function.
Turn the head during swallowing to redirect bolus flow.
explanation:
Swallowing rehabilitation aims to change what the muscles or neural pathways can do over time. **Repeated, targeted exercise can improve the physiological function of the swallowing muscles.**

**A. Adjust mealtime lighting and cueing** — Removing distractions or providing an adapted cup can make a meal safer while the impairment persists.
**B. Change bolus volume or consistency** — Adjusting viscosity, texture or size changes the demands of the current swallow.
**C. Train swallowing muscles to improve physiologic function** — A tongue-strengthening program trains pressure generation for bolus propulsion. Choose the target from the movement deficit seen on assessment.
**D. Turn the head during swallowing to redirect bolus flow** — A head turn can redirect flow toward the stronger pharyngeal channel immediately. Its benefit depends on assuming that position.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 448–450, compensatory and rehabilitative interventions.

q: An 88-year-old man in rehabilitation has lost weight and eats little. He dislikes his restrictive diet but eats preferred foods well. No swallowing disorder is found. Which food-based approach matches Hazzard recommendations for improving oral intake?
o: Offer preferred foods and minimize restrictions with dietitian support
Offer less-preferred foods and maintain restrictions with dietitian support
Reduce meal frequency and maintain restrictions with dietitian support
Narrow the choice of foods and strengthen restrictions with dietitian support
explanation:
The most informative finding is that he eats well when offered food he likes. **Work with the dietitian to offer preferred foods and remove restrictions that no longer justify their nutritional cost.**

**A. Preferred foods and fewer restrictions** — This uses his demonstrated ability and willingness to eat. Monitor intake and weight after changing the menu.
**B. Less-preferred foods, same restrictions** — Dietitian involvement alone does not correct the barrier if the menu stays unappealing.
**C. Fewer meals, same restrictions** — This reduces his opportunities to eat without improving palatability.
**D. Narrower menu, tighter restrictions** — Both changes make it harder to select a tolerable meal.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 427, Table 30-11 and strategies to enhance intake.

q: An 82-year-old man with metastatic colorectal cancer is considering capecitabine. Which statement is supported by Hazzard without assuming that it is superior to every alternative regimen for him?
o: Its efficacy is lower than intravenous 5-FU with leucovorin
It is an oral 5-FU prodrug with similar efficacy
It improves quality of life over 5-FU in frail older adults
Its results in older adults are inferior to those in younger adults
explanation:
Capecitabine is converted to fluorouracil in the body. **It is an oral 5-FU prodrug with efficacy similar to the intravenous 5-FU–leucovorin regimen studied** in metastatic colorectal cancer.

**A. Lower efficacy.** The specified comparison found comparable efficacy, not a consistent disadvantage.
**B. Oral prodrug, similar efficacy.** Route and tolerability can influence selection even when activity is similar.
**C. Improved quality of life in frail adults.** FOCUS2 did not show a quality-of-life advantage for capecitabine over 5-FU.
**D. Inferior results in older adults.** Observed outcomes in older groups appeared similar to those in younger adults, with individual suitability still important.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1443.

optionRationales.body: . Lower efficacy.** The specified comparison found comparable efficacy, not a consistent disadvantage.
. Oral prodrug, similar efficacy.** Route and tolerability can influence selection even when activity is similar.
. Improved quality of life in frail adults.** FOCUS2 did not show a quality-of-life advantage for capecitabine over 5-FU.
. Inferior results in older adults.** Observed outcomes in older groups appeared similar to those in younger adults, with individual suitability still important.

explanationParts.text: Capecitabine is converted to fluorouracil in the body. **It is an oral 5-FU prodrug with efficacy similar to the intravenous 5-FU–leucovorin regimen studied** in metastatic colorectal cancer.

q: An older adult has predominant progressive behavior and personality changes, with relatively little episodic-memory complaint. Which interpretation is supported by Hazzard’s discussion of bvFTD?
o: The pattern localizes primarily to the occipital lobes rather than frontal regions
The pattern points toward frontal or anterior temporal involvement
The absence of prominent amnesia makes a neurodegenerative disorder unlikely
The emergence of memory loss would rule out the diagnosis of bvFTD
explanation:
Behavioral-variant FTD often presents through declining social judgment and personality change. **Prominent progressive behavior change points toward frontal or anterior temporal involvement**.

**A. Occipital localization.** Occipital disease more typically produces visual or perceptual symptoms.
**B. Frontal or anterior temporal.** These regions support empathy, inhibition and social conduct.
**C. No amnesia excludes degeneration.** Neurodegenerative syndromes need not begin with memory loss.
**D. Later amnesia rules out FTD.** Memory can become affected during the illness.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 982.

. Frontal or anterior temporal.** These regions support empathy, inhibition and social conduct.
. No amnesia excludes degeneration.** Neurodegenerative syndromes need not begin with memory loss.
. Later amnesia rules out FTD.** Memory can become affected during the illness.

q: An older adult has recurrent spontaneous lobar hemorrhages and numerous strictly lobar microbleeds. Which cause fits this distribution best?
o: Hypertensive deep perforator arteriopathy
Rupture of a deep lenticulostriate aneurysm
Cerebral amyloid angiopathy of cortical vessels
Hemorrhage confined to a pontine cavernoma
explanation:
Cerebral amyloid deposition affects cortical and leptomeningeal vessels and predisposes to lobar hemorrhage. Hypertensive small-vessel disease more commonly produces deep hemorrhages and microbleeds.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, Ch63, p994.

q: Are local coverage determinations strict hospice admission requirements?
o: Yes - meeting an LCD removes the need for terminal-illness certification
No - they guide prognosis and are not hospice admission requirements
No - they concern neither prognosis nor eligibility
Yes - they replace physician prognostic judgment
explanation:
A US hospice local coverage determination gives clinicians guidance about findings compatible with a limited prognosis. Medicare still requires an individualized physician certification.
**Use the LCD to inform prognosis. Its listed clinical indicators are guidance for assessing eligibility.**

**A. Replaces certification** Meeting listed indicators still requires appropriate physician certification.
**B. Guides prognosis** The clinician can use the pattern of decline and other supporting findings when explaining the prognosis.
**C. Unrelated to prognosis** Helping to assess an expected survival of six months or less is precisely the purpose of the disease-specific indicators.
**D. Replaces judgment** A checklist cannot capture every terminal trajectory or substitute for the clinician's documented reasoning.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1046. CMS, Medicare Benefit Policy Manual, ch. 9, §20.1.

q: What makes podocyte loss important in the proposed sclerosis mechanism?
o: Damaged podocytes are postmitotic cells without the capacity for replacement
Complete glomerular sclerosis preserves the affected nephron and its filtration capacity
Podocyte detachment maintains basement-membrane coverage and protects against glomerular sclerosis
Podocytes multiply in proportion to the enlargement of the glomerular tuft
explanation:
**Mature podocytes have very limited capacity to replace lost cells**. As the glomerular tuft enlarges, remaining podocytes must cover more basement membrane. Detachment exposes segments to adhesion and sclerosis.

**A. Postmitotic podocytes.** Limited regenerative capacity makes cell loss a critical event in the proposed pathway.
**B. Sclerosis preserves filtration.** Complete glomerulosclerosis eliminates filtration by the affected nephron.
**C. Detachment preserves coverage.** Detachment instead leaves areas of basement membrane uncovered.
**D. Proliferation matches tuft growth.** Surviving cells may hypertrophy, but they cannot reliably expand in number to match the surface area.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, Ch 82, p. 1272.

optionRationales.body: . Postmitotic podocytes.** Limited regenerative capacity makes cell loss a critical event in the proposed pathway.
. Sclerosis preserves filtration.** Complete glomerulosclerosis eliminates filtration by the affected nephron.
. Detachment preserves coverage.** Detachment instead leaves areas of basement membrane uncovered.
. Proliferation matches tuft growth.** Surviving cells may hypertrophy, but they cannot reliably expand in number to match the surface area.

explanationParts.text: **Mature podocytes have very limited capacity to replace lost cells**. As the glomerular tuft enlarges, remaining podocytes must cover more basement membrane. Detachment exposes segments to adhesion and sclerosis.

q: איזה מהבאים היא אינדיקציה לטיפול בכריתת בלוטת יותרת התריס (Parathyroidectomy) באנשים מבוגרים עם היפרפאראתירואידיזם ראשוני?
o: צפיפות עצם עם T- Score פחות ממינוס 1
Calcium Score גבוה ב- CT קורונרים
איסוף שתן לסידן מעל 400 מ"ג ל- 24 שעות
סימני Chvostek Sign ו- Trousseau Sign
keySource: IMA 2025-Jun Basic official answer key after appeals, Q122
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders
explanation:
Parathyroid surgery treats autonomous PTH secretion when hypercalcemia or organ involvement makes definitive treatment appropriate. **A 24-hour urinary calcium above 400 mg represents marked hypercalciuria and is a renal indication for surgery.**

**A. T-score below minus one** — This broad cutoff includes mild osteopenia. The relevant skeletal criteria include osteoporosis or vertebral fracture.
**B. High coronary calcium score** — Coronary artery calcification measures atherosclerotic burden and does not substitute for renal imaging or urinary calcium.
**C. Urinary calcium above 400 mg per day** — This exceeds the sex-specific thresholds of 250 mg/day in women and 300 mg/day in men.
**D. Chvostek and Trousseau signs** — These signs of neuromuscular irritability suggest hypocalcemia.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1539, Table 97-10. Fifth International Workshop on Primary Hyperparathyroidism (2022), surgical recommendations.
